question: A 30-year-old woman presents with her fourth episode of painful grouped genital vesicles in 18 months. Each episode has been milder and shorter than the first. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of her recurrent genital herpes?

answers.text: Reactivation of latent HSV from the sacral dorsal root ganglia triggered by stress or immunosuppression

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. After primary genital infection, HSV undergoes retrograde axonal transport to the sacral dorsal root ganglia (S2–S4) where it establishes lifelong latency. Triggers such as stress, fever, menstruation, or immunosuppression induce reactivation — the virus travels anterograde along sensory nerves back to the genital epithelium, causing lesions that are progressively milder due to pre-existing immunity.

answers.text: Reinfection with a new strain of HSV-2 from sexual contacts each time

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Recurrent episodes result from reactivation of the patient's own latent virus, not repeated reinfection with new strains. The decreasing severity with each recurrence is characteristic of reactivation in the presence of mounting host immunity.

answers.text: Persistent active viral replication in the genital epithelium between clinical episodes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Between clinical episodes, HSV is latent in the sacral ganglia with no active epithelial replication (though intermittent asymptomatic shedding can occur). Active mucosal replication resumes only during clinical recurrences.

answers.text: Progressive autoimmune inflammation of genital mucosa triggered by the initial HSV infection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Recurrent genital herpes is caused by viral reactivation, not autoimmune inflammation. The vesicles contain infectious virus demonstrable by PCR or viral culture, confirming an infectious rather than autoimmune aetiology.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the HSV latency–reactivation cycle: primary infection → retrograde transport to sacral ganglia → latency → reactivation (triggered by stress, fever, immunosuppression) → anterograde transport → recurrent genital lesions.

HSV establishes lifelong latency in the sacral dorsal root ganglia after primary infection. Reactivation triggers anterograde axonal transport back to the genital epithelium, causing recurrent lesions that are milder due to pre-existing partial immunity.
